description: We are a two-person team from Maldonado, Uruguay, participating through the Punta del Este local event. Enzo is an IT student at Universidad Católica del Uruguay with experience in data analytics, automation and software development. Yazmin is an IT student at the same university, brings a background in sales and client communication, leading storytelling, content and presentation.
summary:
Still There (Siguen Ahí) is an interactive web game that turns kids aged 9-12 into space explorers who discover the machines NASA left behind on the Moon and Mars.

Players choose a world and explore real NASA Solar System Treks maps, where each pin marks a machine at its real coordinates: the Apollo 11 laser retroreflector, the Apollo 15 Lunar Roving Vehicle, the Opportunity rover and the Ingenuity helicopter. They find each machine on real orbital photos, read its story told in first person, answer a short challenge and collect its card, unlocking the next machine along the way.

These machines made today’s space exploration possible, but their stories are hidden in technical archives that few kids ever read. Still There turns real NASA data into short, playful stories, with a visible source for every fact. It works in Spanish and English on simple school laptops, and adding new machines or worlds only means adding new data. Our goal: a new generation that knows these forgotten heroes and wants to explore further.
details:
What does it do and how does it work?

Still There (Siguen Ahí) is a bilingual web game for kids aged 9–12 about the machines NASA left behind on the Moon and Mars. The player chooses a world and explores a real NASA map, where each pin marks a machine at its real location. Tapping a pin opens a short story told in first person by the machine itself ("I was supposed to last 90 days…"), next to a real NASA photo. Each story ends with a challenge question, so the player has to remember the facts. Our prototype includes four machines: the Apollo 11 Laser Retroreflector, the Apollo 15 Lunar Roving Vehicle, the Opportunity rover and the Ingenuity helicopter.

What benefits does it have?

It turns "space junk" into heroes with a story. Kids learn real science (for example, that the Moon moves away from Earth about 3.8 cm every year) in a few minutes, without reading long texts. It runs in any browser, on a phone, tablet or computer, with no installation, login or registration. It works in English and Spanish, so kids in Latin America can use it in their own language.

What is the intended impact?

We want kids to understand that the objects left on the Moon and Mars are not trash: they are part of human history and some of them still do science today. We also want them to think about space sustainability: if we leave things behind, we should know what they are, where they are and why they matter. In the future, the same format can grow into a full app with more machines, user progress and a guide for teachers.

What tools did we use?

HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with the Leaflet library for the maps. Maps come from NASA Solar System Treks (LRO WAC mosaic for the Moon, Viking MDIM 2.1 color mosaic for Mars). Photos come from the NASA Image and Video Library. The demo is hosted on GitHub Pages. We designed the presentation in Canva; the AI-generated illustrations are marked with a watermark. We used Claude (Anthropic) to help write the demo code, based on our design and content.

How is it creative?

The machines tell their own stories. Instead of a list of dates, kids "meet" a mirror, a car, a rover and a helicopter, each with its own voice and personality. The stories are imagined, but every fact in them comes from NASA sources. The real map gives the feeling of being an explorer looking for the machines on another world.

What factors did we consider?

- Age: short sentences, one idea per scene, big buttons and simple questions.

- Accuracy: we only used facts we could check in NASA sources.

- Language: English and Spanish, because our target users in Uruguay and Latin America speak Spanish.

- Access: no login, no installation and low data use, so it works on school computers and phones.

- Scope: we kept the prototype small (four machines) so that it works well, and we can add more machines later.
